newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil faces legal race to prevent Indian clash.
newsitem.headline: Brazil faces legal race to prevent Indian clash.

text.p: A Brazilian government lawyer on Monday said she faced a race against time to prevent bloodshed on an Indian reservation where tribe members have vowed to die rather than leave land they consider sacred.
About 200 Guarani-Kaiowa Indians in the western state of Mato Grosso do Sul were given a Wednesday deadline to obey a court order and leave their village that lies inside a private cattle ranch.

But the Indians have said they will fight to their death or commit suicide if police try to remove them from the area that includes three ancient cemeteries and has been officially recognised as an Indian reservation.
"There is a very strong possibility there will be violence. Deaths are likely," said federal attorney Ana Lucia Amaral, who is trying to overturn the eviction order.

About 150 Guarani-Kaiowas have joined some 70 nearby villagers to face any police operation to clear the land, Maucir Paulette, a lawyer with the Catholic Church's Indian Missionary Council (CIMI) said.

The Indians were armed with guns as well as traditional clubs and bows and arrows, and have stockpiled about 15 gallons (60 liters) of gasoline that they could use for Molotov cocktails or to set fire to themselves, he said.
"The decision to stay put was taken at a meeting of leaders and they will not change their minds. They are not bluffing when they say they will fight," Paulette said.
He travelled to the village over the weekend and said some Indians had daubed themselves in warpaint and had taken up positions in and around the area.

A court official where the order was issued said the judge was merely following the decision of a more senior tribunal, which upheld an appeal by the landowner of the demarcation of the area as a reservation.

A first appeal by the government of the eviction order was lost when two members of a three-judge appeals tribunal in Sao Paulo rejected the case. The government was waiting for the third judge to announce his already irrelevent ruling before lodging a high court appeal in Brasilia, Amaral said.
"Unfortunately, some judges spend all their lives locked in their offices and have no understanding of the urgency of a case like this," she said.

The Kaiowas and the Guaranis were once flourishing tribes who roamed a vast region of Brazil and what is now Paraguay. As settlers pushed deeper into Brazil's interior, the groups were pushed into ever more remote corners of the country. They live in poverty in small areas surrounded by huge farms.
